name: Toraja-Sadan
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source.
catalog_quote: Stress is a rather complex phenomenon in /'kesu?/ and a full description falls outside the scope of this paper. We therefore confine ourselves to a few general remarks. The place of the stress is distinctive: /'talomo/ 'he has lost' /ta'lomo/ 'we go, let's go' ... In general the stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the word base and remains there in case of suffixation and/or prefixation. …

new_statements.quote: [p.62] 2.8 Tekanan. Tekanan dalam bahasa Toraja tampaknya fonemis. Jadi, di samping fonem segmental ada juga suprasegmental yang meliputi tekanan, kuantitas, jeda dan intonasi. [p.63] Tekanan kata dalam bahasa ini yang cukup menarik ditemukan pada kata-kata seperti berikut: /kan'demi/ 'makanan kamu' /kandemi'/ 'makanlah' /'talomo/ 'dia sudah kalah' /ta'lomo/ 'mari kita pergi' /'alai/ 'ambil itu' /a'lai/ 'rampas' /'ulaiq/ 'ikutlah dia' /u'laiq/ 'usirlah dia'. Selain hal-hal yang tercatat di atas, dapat dikemukakan bahwa yang umum dalam bahasa Toraja ialah tekanan, biasanya jatuh pada suku kedua dari akhir kata dasar walaupun bentuk dasarnya itu mendapat awalan atau akhiran. Contoh: /'tiro/ 'lihat' /paq'tiro/ 'dukun' /pa'tiro/ 'yang melihat' /'tironaq/ 'lihat saya' /maqpope'tiro/ ... /'uruqmi/ 'silakan urut' /pe'uruq/ ... /di'uruq/ 'dia diurut' /pe'uruqna/ 'pengurutnya'
new_statements.translation: [p.62] 2.8 Stress. Stress in Toraja appears to be phonemic. So, besides the segmental phonemes there are also suprasegmentals comprising stress, quantity, juncture and intonation. [p.63] Word stress in this language that is quite interesting is found in words such as the following: /kan'demi/ 'your food' /kandemi'/ 'eat!' /'talomo/ 'he has lost' /ta'lomo/ 'let us go' /'alai/ 'take that' /a'lai/ 'seize' /'ulaiq/ 'follow him' /u'laiq/ 'drive him away'. Apart from the things noted above, it can be stated that what is general in Toraja is that stress usually falls on the second syllable from the end of the base word, even when that base receives a prefix or a suffix. Examples: /'tiro/ 'see' /paq'tiro/ 'healer' /pa'tiro/ 'the one who sees' /'tironaq/ 'see me' /maqpope'tiro/ ... /'uruqmi/ 'please massage' /pe'uruq/ ... /di'uruq/ 'he is massaged' /pe'uruqna/ 'his masseur/massaging tool'.

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog's StressTyp2 record (penultimate: penultimate stress), but specifies the domain as the base word: prefixes are irrelevant and the endings exemplified (=naq, =mi, possessive -na) leave stress on the base penult, yielding surface pairs the authors call 'apparently phonemic'. This matches Sande & Stokhof 1977 and the 1997 Tata Bahasa Toraja (penult, clitics unstressed and non-shifting) already noted in, except that 1984 writes /pe'uruqna/ (possessive -na not shifting) where the 1997 grammar counts possessive suffixes inside the stress domain.
new_statements.rule_in_words: General rule: stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the base word (kata dasar) and stays on that syllable when prefixes are added and, in the examples given, when endings such as =naq 'me', =mi and -na follow (/'tironaq/, /'uruqmi/, /pe'uruqna/, i.e. surface antepenult in those forms). The authors hedge that stress 'appears to be phonemic', citing surface pairs like /'talomo/ 'he has lost' vs /ta'lomo/ 'let's go' and /kan'demi/ 'your food' vs /kandemi'/ 'eat!', which differ in morphological make-up (suffix vs enclitic) rather than in the root.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing on secondary stress in the recovered pages (pp. 19-77).
new_statements.exceptions: Surface contrasts /kan'demi/~/kandemi'/, /'talomo/~/ta'lomo/, /'alai/~/a'lai/, /'ulaiq/~/u'laiq/ presented as evidence that stress 'seems phonemic'; endings in the example list (=naq, =mi, -na) do not attract or shift stress, so affixed/cliticised words can surface with antepenultimate stress. 'biasanya' (usually) signals the penult rule is a default, not exceptionless.
new_statements.identity_note: The work describes bahasa Toraja Sa'dan (South Sulawesi) as a whole; sec. 2.7 (p. 62) lists local dialect variants (/daraŋ/~/naraŋ/~/dyaraŋ/ 'horse', /wai/~/bui/~/wi/~/woi/ 'water') without tying the stress statement to a particular dialect. Only printed pp. 19-77 of the 142-page book were recoverable.

audit.action: a better source should be cited for the same classification
audit.recode_to: Keep penultimate (penultimate stress) and dominant-set membership; strict-set membership is defensible under the 1997 analysis (clitics outside the word) but should carry the stated sub-rule that prefixed monosyllabic roots keep root stress (word-final: meséng, maqrók, dirók) and S&S's final-stressed contracted/expressive items (/a'lan/, /ba?'bak/). If the catalog's 'no rule-level exceptions' test counts clause (c) as a rule-level exception, move to fixed-dominant; otherwise no reclassification.
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote: verbatim on S&S 1977 printed p.22 in the PDF we hold (page scan checked), locator correct; but the record's own quote/cite/loc/grade fields are blank — the passage sits only in the domain-quote and sources fields. (2) Deciding source: a 1977 structuralist phonology article by a native-speaker linguist, impressionistic; the fuller 1997 Pusat Bahasa grammar by the same author is held and states the rule more strongly ('dapat diramalkan.. suku kedua dari belakang', pp.59, 190) with affixed, reduplicated and compound examples, clitics explicitly unstressed and outside the domain (p.61, 194), and one stated sub-regularity (monosyllabic roots keep stress under prefixation, p.60, 194(c)). Both sources agree on penultimate stress over root+affixes; S&S's 'distinctive' minimal pairs are suffix-vs-enclitic pairs, which the 1997 grammar resolves. No instrumental or later phonological stu
